slides.title: Learning Objective
slides.text:
Learning Objective

•  By the end of this lecture, students will be able to:
   – Understand degrees of freedom (DOF) and the role of different links and joints
        in a manipulator
   – Construct and interpret a homogeneous transformation
       matrices.
   – Apply Denavit-Hartenberg (DH) parameters to determine
        transformation matrices for robotic manipulators.
   – Perform forward kinematics analysis for robotic manipulators.
   – Analyze the kinematics of the Unimation PUMA 560
       manipulator.
   – Understand the model of the differential drive mobile
       robots.
   – Derive and apply the kinematic equations of a differential
        drive mobile robot.

slides.title: Introduction
slides.text:
Introduction

•  Robots are designed to perform tasks that require precise motion, positioning,
   and manipulation.
•  Robotic systems include manipulators (robot arms) and mobile robots used for
   navigation and transportation tasks.
•  Robotic manipulators consist of rigid links connected by joints, forming a
   kinematic chain that enables controlled motion.
•  Mobile robots, such as differential drive robots, use wheel velocities to control
   their motion and navigation.





                                                                                                           4

slides.title: Kinematics
slides.text:
Kinematics

•   It is the study of motion that treats the motion without regard to the
   forces that cause it.
•   It studies the position, the velocity, the acceleration, and all higher-order
   derivatives of the position variables w.r.t. time or other variables.
•  Using kinematics, we will study the relationship between joint angles
  and the position of the end-effector.
•  To describe robot motion mathematically, coordinate
   frames are assigned to each link of the robot.
•  The study of manipulator kinematics involves,
  among other things, how the locations of these
   frames change as the mechanism articulates



                                                                                                           5

slides.title: Why FK Matters for AI in Robotics
slides.text:
Why FK Matters for AI in Robotics

•  Reinforcement Learning agents use FK to translate policy outputs (joint
   commands) into Cartesian observations.
•  Imitation Learning datasets store demonstrations as joint trajectories; FK maps
  them to the task space.
•  Motion planning algorithms use FK at every node to check collision geometry.
•   Differentiable FK enables gradient-based trajectory optimization and neural
   motion planning.
•  Physics simulators (MuJoCo, Bullet, Isaac) implement FK
    internally for every rendering step.
•  Understanding FK is prerequisite for sim-to-real transfer
    in deep robot learning.




                                                                                                           6

slides.title: Degree of Freedom (DOF)
slides.text:
Degree of Freedom (DOF)

•  The degree of freedom (DOF) of a robotic system is the number of independent
   parameters required to completely describe the position and orientation of the
   system in space.
•   In the context of robotic manipulators, it represents the number of
   independent joint variables that can be controlled to determine the
   configuration of the robot.
•  Degrees of Freedom of a Rigid Body in Space
    –  3 Translational DOF: motion along the X, Y, and Z axes
    –  3 Rotational DOF: rotation about the X, Y, and Z axes
•  DOF in Robotic Manipulators
    –  Each revolute joint contributes one rotational DOF.
    –  Each prismatic joint contributes one translational DOF.
•  DOF determines the maneuverability of the manipulator.


                                                                                                           7

slides.title: Link Description
slides.text:
Link Description

•  A robotic manipulator can be modeled as a set of rigid bodies connected together in
   a chain. These rigid bodies are called links.
•   Joints form a connection between neighbouring pairs of links and constrain their
    relative motion.
•  The majority of industrial manipulators employ one of two basic joint types:
      1.   Revolute joints, in which relative motion is rotational about a fixed axis
      2.   Prismatic joints, in which relative motion is translational along a fixed axis
•   Links are numbered starting from the fixed base of the
   manipulator.
    –  The immobile base is designated as link 0.
    –  The first moving link is labelled link 1, and numbering continues
         sequentially.
    –  The last link in the chain, link n, is the free end of the arm and
          typically carries the end-effector
•  Most industrial manipulators therefore have five or six joints


                                                                                                           8

slides.title: Joint Type
slides.text:
Joint Type

•  The term lower pair is used to describe a joint in which relative
  motion occurs through direct surface contact between two bodies.
•  The 6 possible lower-pair
     1.  Revolute (R, 1-DOF)
     2.  Prismatic (P, 1-DOF)
     3.  Screw (R, 1-DOF)
     4.   Cylindrical (P+R, 2-DOF)
     5.  Planar (P-P-R, 3-DOF)
     6.   Spherical (R-R-R, 3-DOF)




                                                                                                           9

slides.title: Denavit–Hartenberg Parameters
slides.text:
Denavit–Hartenberg Parameters

•  The Denavit–Hartenberg method provides a systematic way to
   assign coordinate frames and describe the geometry of serial
   manipulators using a minimal set of parameters.
•  Describing relative motion using only 4 parameters per joint
   –  link length 𝑎, link twist 𝛼, link offset 𝑑, and joint angle, 𝜃
•  They allow us to:
   – Model position and orientation of each robot link
   – Systematically derive kinematic equations
   – Convert a complex 3D mechanical structure into
       simple mathematical matrices


                                                                                                          10

slides.title: Denavit–Hartenberg Parameters (Cont.)
slides.text:
Denavit–Hartenberg Parameters (Cont.)

•  The kinematic function of a link is to maintain a fixed geometric
   relationship between the two joint axes that it supports. This
   relationship is completely described by two parameters: the link
   length, 𝑎, and the link twist, 𝛼.





                                                                                                          11

   links.

slides.title: Frame Assignment Rules
slides.text:
Frame Assignment Rules

     1.   Identify the joint axes and imagine infinite lines along them from steps 2
        through 5 below, consider two of these neighboring lines (at axes i and i+1).
     2.   Identify the common perpendicular between them, or point of intersection. At
        the point where the common perpendicular meets the i-axis, assign the link-
        frame origin.
     3.   Assign the 𝑧𝑖 axis pointing along the i-joint axis.
     4.   Assign the 𝑥𝑖 axis pointing along the common perpendicular, or, if the axes
          intersect, assign 𝑥𝑖 to be normal to the plane containing the two axes.
     5.   Assign the 𝑦𝑖 axis to complete a right-hand coordinate
         system.
     6.   Assign {0} to match {1} when the first joint variable is
          zero. For {N} choose an origin location and 𝑥𝑁 direction
           freely, but generally so as to cause as many linkage
        parameters as possible to become zero.



                                                                                                          15

slides.title: Differential Drive Robot
slides.text:
Differential Drive Robot

•  A differential drive robot is a mobile robot
   that uses two independently driven wheels
   placed on either side of its body to move
  and steer.
•  A differential drive robot has:
   – Two independently driven wheels
   – Distance between wheels = 2d
   – Wheel radius = r
   – Robot heading angle = 𝜙
   –  Left wheel linear velocity = 𝑣𝑙= 𝑟𝑢𝑙
   –  Right wheel linear velocity = 𝑣𝑟= 𝑟𝑢𝑟
   –  𝑢𝑙, 𝑢𝑟 are angular velocities of left and right
      wheel respectively


                                                                                                          20

slides.title: Kinematics of Differential Drive Robot
slides.text:
Kinematics of Differential Drive Robot

•  Unlike a manipulator arm, a differential drive robot move on a flat
   plane(ground).
•   Its forward kinematic maps wheel velocities -> robot body velocity ->
   change in pose(x, y, 𝜙) where:
   –  x, y = robot position in the plane
   – 𝜙= robot heading angle
•  Forward kinematics for a differential-drive robot tells you how the
   robot’s position and orientation change when the left and right wheels
   rotate.
•  Two main advantages of a diff-drive robots are
   –  Its simplicity due to motor directly attached to the axle of each wheel.
   – High maneuverability, root can spin in place by rotating the wheel in opposite
        directions.


                                                                                                          22

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  The Denavit–Hartenberg convention provides a systematic
  method for assigning frames
• A minimum of six joints (DOF) is required to fully position and
   orient an end-effector in 3D space.
•  Forward kinematics determines the end-effector pose from joint
   variables.
•  Differential drive robots use an independent
  wheel velocities for motion.
•  Kinematic models enable analysis, simulation,
  and control of robotic systems.



                                                                                                          24
